items.name: First peoples & early villages
items.description: Hunter-gatherers reached the Guatemalan highlands by the end of the Ice Age; obsidian and Clovis-style points come from sites such as Los Tapiales in Totonicapán. Maize farming spread through the Archaic, and by about 1800–1500 BCE pottery-using villages appeared on the Pacific coast (the Locona and Ocós horizons) and in the highlands.

items.name: Kaminaljuyu, highland city of the Valley of Guatemala
items.description: Kaminaljuyu, now under Guatemala City, grew from a village into the great highland Maya centre of the Late Preclassic (about 400 BCE–100 CE), with irrigation canals from Lake Miraflores, carved stelae and control of the El Chayal obsidian source. In the Early Classic it built Teotihuacan-style talud-tablero platforms and tombs, a sign of close ties with the central Mexican city. It declined after about 800 and was abandoned by about 1200.

items.name: El Mirador & the Preclassic Petén
items.description: In the far north of Petén, Nakbe and then El Mirador rose as the first great Maya cities, with La Danta among the largest pyramids ever built and causeways (sacbeob) linking the Mirador Basin. Lidar surveys since 2016 show dense Preclassic settlement and earthworks. El Mirador was largely abandoned around 150 CE.

items.name: Mutal (Tikal), Classic Maya kingdom
items.description: Tikal, whose kings called their realm Mutal, was one of the two great Classic Maya powers. Its dynasty traced itself to Yax Ehb Xook (about 90 CE). In 378 Siyaj K’ak’ arrived from Teotihuacan and installed a new king. After defeat by Caracol in 562 came a long hiatus, until Jasaw Chan K’awiil I beat Calakmul in 695 and Tikal rebuilt its great temples. Its last dated monument is from 869.

items.name: Dos Pilas, Aguateca & the Petexbatún
items.description: A breakaway branch of Tikal’s royal family founded Dos Pilas in the south-west of Petén around 629 under B’alaj Chan K’awiil, who sided with Calakmul against Tikal. The Petexbatún kingdom grew to rule Seibal and the Pasión river trade. After Dos Pilas fell in 761 the court moved to fortified Aguateca, which was burned and abandoned around 810, an early sign of the Classic collapse.

items.name: Quiriguá & the Motagua valley
items.description: Quiriguá, in the lower Motagua valley, was founded as a dependency of Copán (426). In 738 its king K’ak’ Tiliw Chan Yopaat captured and beheaded Copán’s ruler Uaxaclajuun Ub’aah K’awiil, and Quiriguá became an independent city whose giant sandstone stelae and zoomorphs are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its last monuments date to about 810.

items.name: The Classic Maya collapse
items.description: Between about 760 and 950 the southern lowland kingdoms stopped raising dated monuments and their cities emptied. Warfare, drought, deforestation and the failure of divine kingship all played a part. Tikal’s last stela dates to 869. People stayed around the Petén lakes, while power shifted north to Yucatán and to the highlands.

items.name: The K’iche’ kingdom of Q’umarkaj
items.description: The K’iche’ built the strongest Postclassic highland kingdom, with its capital at Q’umarkaj (Utatlán) near Santa Cruz del Quiché, and recorded their own origins and kings in the Popol Vuh. Under K’iq’ab (about 1425–1475) they conquered the Quetzaltenango valley and the cacao-rich Pacific piedmont and held the Kaqchikel as allies, until a revolt around 1470 split the realm. Pedro de Alvarado defeated the K’iche’ in February 1524 and burned Q’umarkaj in March.

items.name: The Kaqchikel kingdom of Iximche
items.description: Around 1470 the Kaqchikel broke away from the K’iche’ and founded their own capital at Iximche. They allied with Alvarado in 1524, and the first Spanish capital, Santiago, was founded at Iximche that July. Spanish demands for tribute set off a Kaqchikel revolt in August 1524 that lasted until their surrender in 1530. The Annals of the Kaqchikels record these years from the Maya side.

items.name: Tz’utujil, Mam & the other highland nations
items.description: Other Maya nations held the rest of the highlands. The Tz’utujil ruled the south shore of Lake Atitlán from Chiya’ and the cacao coast below it until Alvarado defeated them in April 1524. The Mam held the north-west from Zaculeu, which fell to Gonzalo de Alvarado after a siege in October 1525. Poqomam, Q’eqchi’, Ch’orti’ and non-Maya Pipil and Xinca peoples lived further east and south.

items.name: The Spanish conquest of Guatemala
items.description: Pedro de Alvarado, sent by Cortés from Mexico with Spanish soldiers and thousands of Nahua allies, invaded in 1524 and beat the K’iche’ near Quetzaltenango. Tz’utujil, Pipil, Mam and Kaqchikel resistance followed over the next six years. Epidemics had already struck before the Spanish arrived. The conquest of the lowlands took far longer: Petén’s Itza held out until 1697.

items.name: Tezulutlán becomes Verapaz
items.description: The Q’eqchi’ and Poqomchi’ uplands to the north, which the Spanish called Tezulutlán, the “Land of War”, resisted armed conquest. From 1537 Dominican friars led by Bartolomé de las Casas won the right to bring the region in peacefully, without soldiers. The Crown renamed it Verapaz (“True Peace”) in 1547, and Cobán became its centre.

items.name: The Itza kingdom of Nojpetén
items.description: The Itza, who traced their origins to Chichen Itza in Yucatán, ruled central Petén from Nojpetén, an island city on Lake Petén Itzá (now Flores), with rival Kowoj lands to the north-east. Cortés passed through in 1525, and friars and soldiers failed for nearly two centuries to bring the kingdom under Spanish rule. On 13 March 1697 Martín de Ursúa stormed Nojpetén, ending the last independent Maya kingdom.

items.name: The Kingdom & Captaincy General of Guatemala
items.description: Spanish Central America, from Chiapas to Costa Rica, was ruled from Guatemala as the Kingdom of Guatemala under its own Audiencia (from 1543, seated at Santiago from 1549) and later as a Captaincy General within the Viceroyalty of New Spain. Maya communities were gathered into towns (reducciones), paid tribute and worked under encomienda and repartimiento. Indigo and cacao were the main exports.

items.name: Santiago de los Caballeros (Antigua) & the move to Guatemala City
items.description: The capital moved from Iximche to the Almolonga valley in 1527. After a mudslide from the Volcán de Agua destroyed that city in 1541, it was rebuilt in the Panchoy valley in 1543 as Santiago de los Caballeros, now Antigua Guatemala. The Santa Marta earthquakes of 1773 ruined it, and the Crown moved the capital to Nueva Guatemala de la Asunción, today’s Guatemala City, in 1776.

items.name: Independence, the Federation & Carrera
items.description: Central America declared independence in Guatemala City on 15 September 1821, briefly joined Iturbide’s Mexican Empire (1822–23) and then formed the Federal Republic of Central America (1823–41), with Chiapas lost to Mexico in 1824. Rafael Carrera’s conservative peasant revolt broke up the Federation, and Guatemala became a separate republic in 1847. Carrera ruled until his death in 1865, and Britain kept Belize, whose borders Guatemala disputes to this day.

items.name: Liberal Reform, coffee & United Fruit
items.description: The Liberal Revolution of 1871 brought Justo Rufino Barrios to power. He seized Church and communal Maya lands for coffee estates and brought in forced labour drafts. Dictators followed, including Manuel Estrada Cabrera (1898–1920) and Jorge Ubico (1931–44). The US-owned United Fruit Company came to control huge banana lands, the railways and Puerto Barrios.

items.name: The October Revolution & the 1954 coup
items.description: A popular uprising in October 1944 ended Ubico’s rule and opened ten years of democracy under Juan José Arévalo and Jacobo Árbenz, which brought a labour code, social security and, in 1952, a land reform that took unused United Fruit land. In June 1954 a CIA-backed invasion led by Carlos Castillo Armas overthrew Árbenz.

items.name: The civil war & the Maya genocide
items.description: An army officers’ revolt in 1960 began a 36-year war between military governments and leftist guerrillas. About 200,000 people were killed or disappeared, most of them Maya civilians. The UN-backed truth commission found that state forces committed acts of genocide in the early 1980s, the worst under Efraín Ríos Montt (1982–83). K’iche’ activist Rigoberta Menchú won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992, and the Peace Accords were signed on 29 December 1996.

items.name: Guatemala since the Peace Accords
items.description: After 1996 Guatemala held regular elections, but impunity and corruption persisted. The UN-backed anti-impunity commission CICIG (2007–19) helped bring down President Otto Pérez Molina in 2015. Ríos Montt was convicted of genocide in 2013, though the verdict was annulled. Large-scale migration north and remittances shaped the economy. Anti-corruption candidate Bernardo Arévalo won the 2023 election and took office in January 2024 despite attempts to block him.

sources.title: Wikipedia — International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala
